kernelIdea: r₁e^{iθ₁} · r₂e^{iθ₂} = (r₁r₂)e^{i(θ₁+θ₂)}: multiply lengths, add angles. Comparing e^{i(2θ)} with (e^{iθ})² yields the double-angle formulas; the general version is De Moivre.

kernels.l1: Turn, then turn again. The turns add up.
kernels.l2: If you turn a quarter and then another quarter, you have turned a half. Turns add. That is what multiplying complex numbers does.
kernels.l3: Multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their distances and adds their turns. Multiplying by i is the simplest case: distance unchanged, a quarter turn added.
kernels.l4: Multiplying by i sends the point (a, b) to (−b, a), which is the quarter-turn rule from coordinate geometry — so multiplying by a complex number turns the plane and stretches it.
kernels.l5: Multiplication in polar form multiplies the distances and adds the turns. Raising a point of the unit circle to a whole power multiplies its turn by that power, and reading off the two coordinates gives the multiple-angle identities.
kernels.l6: Multiplication is rotation composed with scaling; De Moivre’s formula (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ is the special case of modulus one.
kernels.l7: Multiplying complex numbers multiplies moduli and adds arguments; De Moivre’s formula follows, and equating real and imaginary parts derives the multiple-angle identities of trigonometry.
kernels.l8: Multiplication makes ℂˣ ≅ ℝ_{>0} × S¹ as topological groups; the nth roots of unity are the finite subgroups of S¹, and their geometry is the cyclic group made visible.
